newsitem.title: UK: Brazil's lead role as raws exporter challenged.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's lead role as raws exporter challenged.

text.p: North Brazil is set to lose its position as Latin America's leading raw sugar supplier early next year, but the extent of tolling by its regional competitors will be unclear for some time, brokers said on Friday.

North Brazilian cargoes should still be available as late as February and even March, depending on current rates of shipment and any delays to the Cuban cane harvest. "We know that they've been shipping at a very fast rate in October and November out of north Brazil," one broker said, adding that one or two U.S. quota vessels had also been chartered to leave from the region.
"So perhaps again it seems to be shipping out rather early and may not leave too much in the Jan/Feb/March position."
Last year north Brazilian producers saw heavy requirements for December and early January shipments as the Cuban crop was delayed, leaving reduced availability for February and March.

Other key regional producers, such as Mexico and Colombia, are preparing to take up the slack and add to the supply. But both countries also produce white sugar in a range of qualities and the amount of raws available for export remains unclear.
"There is a little bit of pressure (on Brazilian premiums) but I don't think it's so much competition as lack of physical interest," said a physical sugar trader.
Cargoes for November/December shipment were offered at 20 points over New York's March raws contract, after trading at around 40 points a couple of weeks ago, market sources said.
Availability of low-quality whites in the region is said to be fairly tight at present, thereby attracting the presence of Brazilian, Colombian and Mexican cargoes.

In its latest report, Czarnikow Sugar said north Brazilian 150 ICUMSA cargoes were trading at discounts of $16 to December, with 100 ICUMSAs offered in Santos at a $12 discount plus $5 expected in port loading disbursements.
Colombia has also entered the market, offering low-quality white sugar and recently selling two cargoes of 150 and 180 ICUMSA sugars for January and February shipment.
Traders said the sales were likely to be older business concluded when the white/raw premium was considerably higher and cited discounts of between $25 and $28 to December.

Most of Colombia's sugar was thought to be tied up with one major trade house, they said. Sri Lanka and Middle East Gulf nations were mentioned as possible destinations for the lower-quality whites as Indian prices were not yet so competitive.
Colombia and Costa Rica have also been conducting regular trade selling raws, with first-quarter cargoes from the latter source trading at premiums of 15 points to New York March.

Equivalent cargoes from Mexico were offered at discounts between $23 and $25 for December/January for 180 ICUMSA quality and $20 bid for 150 ICUMSA. Traders said the level of Mexican raws refining would depend on the whites premium and other factors such as Thai tolling and the extra competition for European sugars from new refineries in the Middle East.

Mexico, along with its regional competitors and major toller Thailand, would only refine raws from national output if world prices for whites were attractive enough. In any case, raw not white sugar would emerge first from their cane harvests.

"The Thais are very quick to produce some more 45 whites when the prices are right so I imagine the opposite will apply," another broker said. "The Mexican season is just about getting going so it will be a little while yet before you get some whites out of there."
Cuba remains the other big unknown in the region. Quoted values for cargoes from the 1996/97 cane crop are weak with a large difference between bid and ask prices.
Traders quoted discounts of 50 points to March raws for first-quarter 1997 Cuban cargoes on the bid side, but said the best offer reported so far was at a discount of 35 points.
